profiles.name: Frederick Shields
profiles.excerpt: Frederick Shields moved between character acting, program hosting and sponsor presentation, making his voice part of both the drama and the commercial structure around it.
profiles.bio_html:
Frederick Shields is best understood as a working radio professional whose assignments crossed the boundaries between acting, hosting and sponsor presentation. His GRH record reaches from westerns and prestige drama to the commercial material that was built directly into sponsored network programming.

That overlap is especially visible on Lux Radio Theatre, where Shields is repeatedly tagged as both performer and commercial spokesman. He also appears as a commercial spokesman on The Abbott and Costello Show and as host on a Screen Directors Playhouse broadcast. Those are distinct microphone jobs, not interchangeable performer labels.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Wild Bill Hickok performances, 12 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits, four Dr. Christian appearances and additional hosting and commercial work. Reliable personal-life documentation remains limited, so GRH keeps the profile centered on those verified broadcast functions.

profiles.name: Red Skelton
profiles.excerpt: Red Skelton turned vaudeville characters into a radio institution, hosting his own network show while creating voices and personalities that later followed him into television.
profiles.bio_html:
Red Skelton came to broadcasting through medicine shows, vaudeville and burlesque, forms that taught him to build comedy around recognizable characters and direct audience response. After national radio appearances in the late 1930s, he became host of Avalon Time and then launched his own NBC program in 1941.

The Red Skelton Show made the host inseparable from the repertory company because Skelton himself supplied many of its recurring personalities. Junior, Clem Kadiddlehopper, Deadeye, San Fernando Red and other characters gave the program a recognizable comic world while the host moved in and out of sketches under his own name. That character system later transferred directly into television.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 92 Red Skelton Show host/performer credits plus a Sealtest Variety Theater appearance. GRH therefore tags Skelton as both performer and host, reflecting the structure of the program listeners actually heard.

profiles.name: Les Tremayne
profiles.excerpt: Les Tremayne became one of radio’s busiest leading men and narrators, moving from First Nighter and The Thin Man to The Whistler and a lifetime of microphone work.
profiles.bio_html:
Les Tremayne was born in London in 1913 and raised in Chicago, where he entered radio at seventeen. His first major break came in 1936 when he replaced Don Ameche on The First Nighter Program. From there he became one of the medium’s most dependable leading men, later playing Nick Charles on The Adventures of the Thin Man and appearing across mystery, comedy and dramatic series.

Tremayne’s smooth, flexible delivery also made him useful as an announcer and narrator. He announced for Bob Crosby, co-hosted The Tremaynes with his then-wife Alice Reinheart and later narrated episodes of The Whistler. His ability to sound conversational while maintaining formal microphone control helped him survive radio’s transition into television and voice work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Whistler narrator/performer credits, six Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances and additional appearances on Sears Radio Theater, CBS Radio Mystery Theater, Inner Sanctum, The Thin Man, The Falcon and This Is Your FBI. He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995.

profiles.name: Stan Waxman
profiles.excerpt: Stan Waxman was a versatile West Coast radio actor whose anthology work also included narration on Escape, adding expository authority to an already broad repertory career.
profiles.bio_html:
Stan Waxman appears across Golden Radio Hour as a West Coast repertory actor whose career was built on range rather than one signature role. His credits span detective drama, westerns, literary anthologies and suspense, the kind of schedule that depended on actors being able to establish a new character almost immediately.

Escape also used Waxman as narrator. On a series that regularly dropped listeners into unfamiliar locations and dangerous situations, narration was part of the dramatic machinery: a voice had to establish place, danger and point of view without slowing the story.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six A Man Called X performances, six Escape narrator/performer credits, five Broadway Is My Beat appearances and additional work on NBC University Theater, Screen Directors Playhouse, Philip Marlowe, Let George Do It and Night Beat. Reliable personal documentation remains limited, so GRH centers his page on that verified repertory and narration record.

profiles.name: Gayne Whitman
profiles.excerpt: Gayne Whitman built a long radio career around cultured narration and adventure leads, from Chandu the Magician to NBC University Theater and documentary-style programs.
profiles.bio_html:
Gayne Whitman was born Alfred D. Vosburgh in Chicago in 1890 and worked in stage, film and radio. Broadcasting became one of his most durable mediums because his polished, authoritative voice could serve equally well in adventure drama, narration and announcing.

Whitman played the title role in Chandu the Magician and later became associated with narrative programs including Strange as It Seems. He also announced Paducah Plantation and narrated radio versions of Lassie, demonstrating how the same voice could move between fictional adventure and factual or storybook framing.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 NBC University Theater narrator/performer credits plus a Screen Directors Playhouse appearance. Those holdings represent only part of a much larger announcing and narration career, so GRH uses the archive count as a preserved sample rather than a total.

profiles.name: Richard Widmark
profiles.excerpt: Richard Widmark began professionally in radio years before Kiss of Death made him a film star, then returned decades later as the Adventure Night host of Sears Radio Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Widmark’s screen breakthrough as Tommy Udo in Kiss of Death can obscure the fact that he entered professional acting through radio. Beginning in the late 1930s, he worked in New York broadcasting and appeared on dramatic programs before Hollywood made his face as recognizable as his voice.

Widmark returned to radio in a different role during the 1979–1980 revival Sears Radio Theater. The anthology assigned a different host and genre to each weekday, and Widmark hosted Adventure Night. That position used his established screen identity to frame new radio dramas rather than casting him simply as another guest actor.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Sears Radio Theater host credits, nine Shadow performances, six Inner Sanctum Mysteries, five Molle Mystery Theatre appearances and additional work on Columbia Workshop, Lux Radio Theatre and other series. His profile therefore connects radio at both ends of his long career.

profiles.name: Martin Wolfson
profiles.excerpt: Martin Wolfson was a New York repertory actor whose wartime and experimental radio work included narration on Words at War alongside mystery and science-fiction roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Martin Wolfson is preserved in Golden Radio Hour primarily as a repertory actor working across New York dramatic radio. His credits include experimental anthology, wartime literary adaptation, mystery and early science fiction rather than one continuing commercial series.

Words at War used Wolfson in narration as well as character performance. That program adapted contemporary books dealing with the war and world affairs, so narrators had to carry factual or literary exposition while maintaining the urgency of a dramatic broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven Columbia Workshop performances, five Words at War narrator/performer credits, three The Mysterious Traveler appearances and additional work on Dimension X, Quiet Please, The Clock and Theater Five. Personal documentation remains scarce, so GRH leaves the profile anchored to that verified radio record.
